Machine learning systemTechnical Field

The presently disclosed subject matter relates to machine learning systems, autonomous device controllers, machine learning methods, and computer readable media.

Background

Neural networks are a popular paradigm for approximating almost any kind of function. The fact that their highly flexible parametric form combined with large amounts of data allows accurate modeling of the underlying tasks generally leads to the most advanced predictive performance. While predictive performance is of course an important aspect, accurate uncertainty estimates regarding predictions are also desirable in many safety critical applications such as autonomous automobiles.

Bayesian neural networks have attempted to impart capabilities to neural networks for modeling uncertainty; they assume a prior distribution over the network weights and, by inference, they can represent their uncertainty in the posterior distribution. However, for such complex models, a priori selection is quite difficult, as understanding the interaction of parameters with data is a significant task. As a result, a priori ease of computation and ease of processing are often employed. Furthermore, reasoning on the weights of neural networks can be a daunting task due to high dimensionality and a posteriori complexity.

An alternative way in which the aforementioned problem can be "bypassed" is to take a stochastic process. They directly assume a distribution over a function (e.g., neural network) without the necessity of resorting to a prior distribution over global parameters such as neural network weights. The Gaussian Process (GP) is an example of a random process. Unfortunately, the gaussian process has two limitations. For example, the underlying model is not very flexible to high dimensional problems and training and reasoning costs are quite high, since it scales cubically with the size of the dataset.

Disclosure of Invention

To address these and other problems, a machine learning system as defined in the claims is presented. The machine learning system is configured to map input data instances to outputs according to a system mapping.

In an embodiment, the output is derived from the second potential input vector in the second potential space by applying a third function to the second potential input vector. A second potential input vector may be determined for the input data instance from a second potential reference vector obtained for a plurality of reference data instances identified as parents of the input data instance. Identifying parent reference data instances may be based on a similarity between a first potential input vector obtained for an input data instance and a first potential reference vector obtained for a set of reference data instances.

Interestingly, the output is derived from a second potential vector in a second potential space. The input instance is not directly mapped to the second potential vector; instead, it is constructed from the reference example associated therewith. The relationship may be determined using the first potential space. This indirect process has the advantage that the system is forced to learn the structure of the input distribution well.

Preferably, the various mappings are random, rather than deterministic. If desired, the mapping can be repeated and averaged to improve accuracy. Various machine learning functions may be applied to the first, second, and third functions. However, neural networks have proven to work particularly well.

Machine learning systems may be used for control of physical systems. For example, the input data instance and the reference data instance may comprise sensor data, in particular images. The output may include an output tag; for example, the system map may be a classification task. Other applications are possible. For example, the system may be trained to predict variables that are difficult to measure directly, e.g., the output may include physical quantities of the physical system, such as temperature, pressure, etc.

Detailed Description

While the presently disclosed subject matter is susceptible of embodiment in many different forms, there are shown in the drawings, and will herein be described in detail, one or more specific embodiments with the understanding that the present disclosure is to be considered as an example of the principles of the presently disclosed subject matter and not intended to limit the presently disclosed subject matter to the specific embodiments shown and described.

Hereinafter, elements of the embodiments are described in operation for the sake of understanding. However, it will be apparent that the respective elements are arranged to perform the functions described as being performed by them.

Furthermore, the presently disclosed subject matter is not limited to the embodiments, and the presently disclosed subject matter lies in each and every novel feature or combination of features described herein or recited in mutually different dependent claims.

The prediction task frequently occurs in computer vision. For example, autonomous device control, e.g., for autonomous cars, depends on decisions based on reliable classification. One problem with predictions made by machine learning systems is that there is often little difference between predictions for situations where the system is well trained and predictions for situations where the system is not well trained. For example, consider a neural network trained to classify landmarks. If the network presents new, previously unseen signposts, the neural network will likely make confident and possibly correct classifications. However, if an image outside the distribution of images used for training, such as an image of a cat, is presented to the neural network, known neural networks tend to still confidently predict landmarks for that image. This is an undesirable behavior and therefore there is a need for a machine learning system that will gracefully fail when presented with such an image, which is referred to as an "out of distribution" o.o.d. image. For example, in an embodiment, the prediction may fall back to or near some default value for points outside of the data distribution.

Other advantages include the possibility of providing a priori knowledge to the model, e.g. specifying inductive bias. For example, nearby instances may be considered more likely to be parents of a given instance. This is much more intuitive than specifying an a priori distribution over global latent variables. The nearby encodings may depend on the particular type of input data. For example, for images, a distance metric, such as an L2 metric, may be used. Other distance metrics may be included if the input data includes other suitable data. For example, in an embodiment, the input data comprises sensor data of a plurality of sensors. For temperature, a temperature difference may be used, for pressure, a pressure difference may be used, and so on. However, the temperature and pressure data may be scaled appropriately to account for the different scales with which they appear in the modeled system. Multiple distance measures may be combined into a single distance, for example by a sum of squares, possibly weighted.

An additional advantage is that the model is forced to learn the dependency structure between data instances. Furthermore, such dependencies can be visualized. Such visualization allows for debugging of the model. Optionally, embodiments may compute and visualize these dependencies. If the clusters shown in the so-called G-map (an example of which is shown in fig. 5) or a-map (these maps are explained further below) are not realistic, the modeler can use this information to further control the machine learning system, for example by increasing or decreasing the number of reference points or by changing a priori knowledge. A further advantage is that in embodiments, a suitable bayesian model can be obtained, which is, for example, exchangeable and consistent under marginalization. This allows probabilistic modeling and inference of underlying information without having to specify a prior distribution over global underlying variables.

A new machine learning system is provided that may be used to train and/or apply machine learnable functions. In an embodiment, two different potential spaces are used, e.g. a multi-dimensional vector space. The elements in these spaces are referred to as the first potential vector and the second potential vector, respectively. A vector may also be referred to as a point in vector space. An output, e.g., a prediction or classification, is made based on the second potential vector. A special set of reference data instances, which may be extracted from the same distribution as the input data instances, are mapped into a second potential space, these being second potential reference vectors.

For training examples other than the reference example, or for input data examples not seen, an indirect approach is used. Both the training data instance and the reference instance are mapped to a first potential space. Thus, the reference data instance corresponds to a vector in a first potential space, for example by a first function, and to a vector in a second potential space, for example by a second function.

In the first potential space, a reference point is selected that is related to the training input instance, e.g., that is similar to the training input instance. Then, points in the second potential space are derived from corresponding points in the second potential space, e.g. averaged, possibly with a weighted average. Finally, the output is calculated from the determined points in the second potential space. Thus, the system calculates the output indirectly from the input by selecting the relevant so-called parent. This forces the system to develop a better understanding of the input distribution structure. This facilitates a better understanding of the distribution of inputs and a better ability to identify unseen inputs that are poorly reflected in the input data.

Note that one or more or all of the mappings may be random. Instead of deterministically determining the output, a probability distribution is determined, and the mapping results are then sampled from the probability distribution. This may be done, for example, for any of a mapping from an input instance to a first potential space, a mapping from a reference instance to a second potential space, a mapping for determining a parent, and a mapping from the second potential space to an output.

There are a number of variations that may be applied in system 300. For example, to derive the second potential vector, the second function B may use the reference tag as an input in addition to the reference point itself. This is indicated in fig. 3a by the dashed line from label 324 to function 340 and in fig. 4 by the dashed line from label 426 to potential space 436. This variant is possible because two potential spaces are used. For unknown inputs, only the mapping to the first potential space is needed, and thus the second potential space may use the label in the mapping. Having the tag as an input in the second potential space increases the predictive power of the second potential space.

To include the label 426 when mapping to the second potential vector, one may use a machine learnable function, such as a neural network, that takes as input both the reference data instance and the label. In a variant, two machine-learnable functions are used, for example two neural networks. The first machine-learnable function may map the reference data instance to a second potential space, and the second machine-learnable function may map the label to the second potential space; then, possibly with the weighting applied, the two second potential vectors may be added or averaged. The weighting factors may be learnable parameters.

Another variation that may be used with or instead of the previous variation is to provide the first potential vector of point 452 as an additional input to the third function 370. This option is illustrated in fig. 3a as a dotted line from the first function 330 to the third function 370. It is found that: adding this additional vector increases the extrapolation capability of the system. On the other hand, without this additional vector, the system more strongly restores the low confidence prediction when equipped with o.o.d. input. Both may be preferred, as appropriate.

An advantage of an embodiment is that the system reverts to or approaches the default output when faced with o.o.d. input. For example, given an o.o.d. input, the input may not have a parent and is therefore mapped onto a default vector in the second potential space. The latter is then mapped to or close to the default output. How close the measured output will be to the default output can be used to determine a confidence in the output.

For example, in an embodiment, the output of unit 370 may include a plurality of output probabilities for a plurality of tags. For example, if the input is a signpost, the output of unit 370 may be a vector indicating a probability for each possible signpost that may be recognized by the system. If a particular output is confidently identified, e.g., a particular signpost, then one probability will be high and the remaining probabilities will be low, e.g., close to zero. If no particular output is confidently identified, many or all of the probabilities will be approximately equal. Thus, confidence in the output can be derived by measuring how close the output is to a coincidence — closer to coincidence, is less confident, and further away from coincidence, is more confident. The confidence that the system has in its output can be reflected in a variety of ways; one way to do this is to calculate the entropy of the generation probability.

In an embodiment, the confidence value may be derived from the unit 370 that does not use the first potential vector as input. The confidence value indicates how well the input is represented among the training inputs. However, the output itself may be taken from unit 370 using the first potential vector as input, so that the output has a better extrapolation.
